title: Retina and receptive fields
text:
CHAPTER 8. VISION
SECTION 8.1. THE RETINA AND RECEPTIVE FIELDS

Why vision?

Vision is the most studied sensory system in neuroscience, and for good reasons. Primates are highly visual animals; a large fraction of the primate cerebral cortex is involved in processing visual information. Visual stimuli are easy to control precisely: you can display any pattern on a screen at any time. And the visual pathway has a clear, roughly hierarchical structure, from the eye to the thalamus to the primary visual cortex and onward. For AI, vision is especially important because the most influential deep learning architectures, convolutional neural networks, were directly inspired by discoveries about the visual system. This chapter follows the path from the retina to the cortex to modern deep networks.

The eye as a camera, and why the analogy fails

The eye resembles a camera. The cornea and lens focus an image onto the retina, a thin layer of neural tissue at the back of the eye. The pupil acts as an adjustable aperture. Kepler described the optical image formation on the retina in 1604, and Descartes is said to have demonstrated it by scraping the back of an ox eye and seeing the inverted image.

But the retina is not a passive film or sensor array. It is a piece of the brain, developmentally an outgrowth of the embryonic forebrain, and it performs substantial computation before any signal leaves the eye. The optic nerve, which carries the retina's output to the brain, contains roughly one million axons in each human eye, while the retina contains on the order of a hundred million photoreceptors. So the retina compresses its input by a factor of around 100. Understanding what it chooses to send, and why, is the first step in understanding vision.

The layers of the retina

The retina has a layered structure, which Cajal drew in exquisite detail. Light passes through the retina (which is mostly transparent) to reach the photoreceptors at the back. Signals then travel forward through the layers:

1. Photoreceptors: rods and cones. Rods are extremely sensitive and work in dim light; they can respond to single photons. Cones work in brighter light and come in three types in most humans, sensitive to long (L, "red"), medium (M, "green"), and short (S, "blue") wavelengths, which underlies color vision. The human retina contains on the order of 90 to 120 million rods and around 5 to 6 million cones, according to commonly cited estimates. Cones are concentrated in the fovea, a small central pit where vision is sharpest; rods are absent from the very center and are densest a little outside it.

2. Bipolar cells: receive input from photoreceptors and pass it to ganglion cells. There are many types, including ON bipolar cells and OFF bipolar cells (explained below).

3. Ganglion cells: the output neurons of the retina, whose axons form the optic nerve. There are dozens of ganglion cell types, each forming a mosaic that covers the visual field and each sending a different "channel" of information to the brain.

4. Horizontal cells and amacrine cells: interneurons that make lateral connections. Horizontal cells connect photoreceptors and bipolar cells over a region, providing lateral inhibition at the first synapse. Amacrine cells (of which there are dozens of types) connect bipolar cells and ganglion cells, contributing to temporal processing, motion detection, and other computations.

Phototransduction

Photoreceptors work in a way that surprises most engineers. In darkness, a photoreceptor is relatively depolarized (around -40 mV), because channels in its outer segment that are kept open by the molecule cyclic GMP allow a steady inward current, called the "dark current." When light is absorbed by the photopigment (rhodopsin in rods), a biochemical cascade is triggered: the activated pigment activates many molecules of a G protein called transducin, each of which activates an enzyme (phosphodiesterase) that breaks down cyclic GMP. The cyclic-GMP-gated channels close, the inward current decreases, and the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes. So photoreceptors respond to light by hyperpolarizing, and they release less neurotransmitter (glutamate) in light than in darkness.

The cascade provides enormous amplification: one photon absorbed can close a measurable fraction of the channels in a rod, which is why rods can detect single photons. Denis Baylor, Trevor Lamb, and King-Wai Yau measured single-photon responses in toad rods in 1979, and in primate rods in the 1980s. The cascade is also an example of a G-protein-coupled receptor signaling pathway (section 6.3); rhodopsin is a GPCR. George Wald received a share of the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on the chemistry of visual pigments, shared with Ragnar Granit and Haldan Keffer Hartline.

Photoreceptors also adapt. Over a range of light intensities spanning many orders of magnitude, from starlight to bright sunlight, the visual system adjusts its sensitivity. This is done partly by switching between rods and cones and partly by adaptation within each cell type and in the retinal circuit. In engineering terms, the retina implements automatic gain control, so that responses encode contrast (relative changes in intensity) rather than absolute intensity.

ON and OFF pathways

Photoreceptors release glutamate onto bipolar cells. Different bipolar cells have different glutamate receptors. OFF bipolar cells have ionotropic glutamate receptors, so they are depolarized by glutamate; since glutamate release decreases in light, OFF bipolar cells hyperpolarize in light and depolarize when light decreases. ON bipolar cells use a metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR6) that, through a G-protein cascade, closes a cation channel when glutamate is bound; so they are hyperpolarized by glutamate and depolarize when light increases (when glutamate release falls). This sign inversion creates two parallel channels: one signaling increments of light (ON) and one signaling decrements (OFF).

Why two channels? One reason is that neurons cannot fire at negative rates. A single channel with a moderate baseline rate could signal increases and decreases, but it would waste energy firing constantly and would have limited range in the downward direction. Splitting the signal into two rectified channels, one for positive changes and one for negative, is more efficient. Engineers will recognize this as similar to push-pull amplifier designs, or to representing a signed signal with two unsigned lines. Notice also the resemblance to the ReLU nonlinearity: an ON cell is roughly a rectified version of the signal, and an OFF cell is a rectified version of its negative.

Hartline and lateral inhibition

The first recordings from single visual neurons were made by Haldan Keffer Hartline, beginning in the early 1930s with the horseshoe crab Limulus, whose compound eye has large photoreceptor units (ommatidia) with accessible nerve fibers. Hartline and colleagues, especially Floyd Ratliff, showed in the 1950s that neighboring units in the Limulus eye inhibit each other: when one unit is illuminated, it reduces the firing of its neighbors. This lateral inhibition enhances contrast at edges. If you illuminate a region with a step edge (bright on one side, dark on the other), units just on the bright side of the edge fire more than units deep in the bright region (because they have fewer bright neighbors inhibiting them), and units just on the dark side fire less than units deep in the dark region. This exaggerates the edge.

Hartline and Ratliff described lateral inhibition with a set of linear equations, now called the Hartline-Ratliff equations:

  r_i = e_i - sum_j k_ij * (r_j - threshold_ij)

where r_i is the response of unit i, e_i is its excitation from light, and k_ij is the strength of inhibition from unit j to unit i (only counting the part of r_j above a threshold). This was one of the first quantitative network models in neuroscience. Lateral inhibition is often used to explain the perceptual illusion called Mach bands, the illusory bright and dark stripes seen at the boundaries of a gradient, described by Ernst Mach in the 1860s, though how much of the illusion is explained by retinal lateral inhibition is debated.

Kuffler and center-surround receptive fields

The concept of the receptive field, the region of the sensory surface in which stimulation affects a neuron's response, was introduced by Sherrington for touch and applied to vision by Hartline, who recorded from single optic nerve fibers in frogs in 1938. In 1953, two papers established the basic properties of retinal ganglion cell receptive fields in vertebrates. Horace Barlow, working in Cambridge, described ganglion cells in the frog retina, including cells that responded best to small dark spots, which he suggested might act as "fly detectors," anticipating the "What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain" paper by Lettvin and colleagues (1959). And Stephen Kuffler, working at Johns Hopkins University, recorded from ganglion cells in the cat retina using small spots of light.

Kuffler found that cat ganglion cells have circular receptive fields with a center and a surrounding annulus that have opposite effects:

- ON-center cells: light in the center excites the cell (increases firing); light in the surround inhibits it. The best stimulus is a small bright spot surrounded by darkness.
- OFF-center cells: light in the center inhibits the cell; light in the surround excites it. The best stimulus is a small dark spot surrounded by light.

Uniform illumination of the whole receptive field produces only a weak response, because center and surround cancel. So these cells respond to local contrast, not to overall brightness. They are, in effect, spot detectors or edge enhancers.

The difference-of-Gaussians model

Robert Rodieck proposed in 1965 a simple mathematical model of the center-surround receptive field: the difference of two Gaussian functions, a narrow, strong one for the center and a broad, weaker one for the surround. In one dimension:

  RF(x) = A_c * exp(-x^2 / (2*sigma_c^2)) - A_s * exp(-x^2 / (2*sigma_s^2))

with sigma_s greater than sigma_c. (In two dimensions, x^2 is replaced by x^2 + y^2.) For an ON-center cell, A_c and A_s are both positive; an OFF-center cell has the opposite sign. If the cell's response is approximately linear for small stimuli, the response to an image I(x, y) is the convolution of the image with the receptive field function (followed by a nonlinearity, such as rectification). The array of ganglion cells thus performs a convolution of the image with a difference-of-Gaussians kernel, sampled at the positions of the ganglion cells.

For a mechatronics student, this is directly familiar from image processing. The difference of Gaussians is a band-pass filter that suppresses both very low spatial frequencies (uniform regions) and very high spatial frequencies (fine noise), passing intermediate frequencies, which emphasize edges and spots. It is closely related to the Laplacian of Gaussian operator used for edge detection by David Marr and Ellen Hildreth in their 1980 theory of edge detection, in which edges are located at the zero crossings of the image filtered by a Laplacian of Gaussian. Marr explicitly connected this to retinal ganglion cell receptive fields.

Why the retina does this: efficient coding

Why should the retina emphasize contrast and discard uniform brightness? In 1961, Horace Barlow proposed the efficient coding hypothesis: sensory systems are designed to transmit as much information as possible about the environment given their limited capacity, by removing redundancy. Natural images are highly redundant: neighboring pixels tend to have similar values. Transmitting each pixel independently would waste capacity on predictable information. A center-surround filter subtracts a local prediction (the surround's average) from each point (the center), transmitting mainly the unpredictable part. This is closely related to predictive coding in signal processing, used in compression schemes such as differential pulse-code modulation, where a predicted value is subtracted before transmission. Mandyam Srinivasan, Simon Laughlin, and Andreas Dubs described the retina's lateral inhibition as predictive coding in 1982.

Joseph Atick and Norman Redlich in the early 1990s showed mathematically that, given the statistics of natural images (whose power spectrum falls off roughly as 1 over spatial frequency squared) and the presence of noise, the optimal linear filter for transmitting information through a limited channel has a center-surround shape at high light levels, and becomes broader and less surround-dominated at low light levels, when noise is high and averaging is more valuable. This matches observations that receptive field surrounds weaken in dim light. Efficient coding remains one of the most successful theoretical principles in sensory neuroscience.

Simon Laughlin also showed in 1981 that the contrast-response function of fly photoreceptor-related neurons (large monopolar cells) matches the cumulative distribution of contrasts in natural scenes, which is the transformation that makes all response levels equally used, maximizing information transmission. This is histogram equalization, a standard technique in image processing, found in a fly's eye.

Parallel channels

The retina does not send one image to the brain; it sends many. In primates, two of the best known ganglion cell types are midget cells, which have small receptive fields, carry color information (red-green opponency), and project to the parvocellular layers of the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus; and parasol cells, which have larger receptive fields, respond to faster changes and lower contrasts, and project to the magnocellular layers. A third group, including small bistratified cells, carries blue-yellow information and projects to koniocellular layers. In mice, whose retinas have been studied in great detail with modern methods, researchers have identified on the order of 30 to 40 or more functionally distinct ganglion cell types, each encoding a different feature of the visual scene: ON or OFF, sustained or transient, direction of motion, local edges, and so on. Tom Baden, Thomas Euler, and colleagues reported in 2016, using calcium imaging, more than 30 functional types in the mouse.

Some ganglion cells are not primarily for image-forming vision. Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) contain their own photopigment, melanopsin, and project to brain areas controlling circadian rhythms and the pupillary reflex. David Berson and colleagues described them in 2002. They explain why some blind people whose rods and cones have degenerated can still entrain their circadian clocks to light.

From retina to cortex

Ganglion cell axons travel through the optic nerve. At the optic chiasm, axons from the nasal half of each retina cross to the other side, so that each side of the brain receives information about the opposite half of the visual field from both eyes. Most axons go to the LGN of the thalamus, which relays information to the primary visual cortex (V1), also called the striate cortex or Brodmann area 17, at the back of the brain. Other axons go to the superior colliculus (involved in eye movements and orienting) and other targets. LGN neurons have center-surround receptive fields similar to those of ganglion cells. The LGN receives more input from the cortex (feedback) than from the retina, suggesting that it is more than a passive relay, though its exact role remains under investigation.

The next step, what happens in V1, is the story of Hubel and Wiesel, told in the next section.

Bridge to AI: the retina as a preprocessing network

The retina offers several lessons for AI and engineering.

Convolution and weight sharing. Every ganglion cell of a given type has roughly the same receptive field shape, centered at a different location. This is exactly a convolution: the same filter applied at every position. Convolutional neural networks use this principle (weight sharing), which dramatically reduces the number of parameters and builds in translation equivariance. The retina had it first.

Learned filters resemble biology. When convolutional networks are trained on natural images, the filters in their first layer often come to resemble center-surround and oriented edge detectors, similar to those found in the retina and V1. In 2019, Jack Lindsey, Samuel Ocko, Surya Ganguli, and Stephane Deny showed that when a deep network modeling the visual system is given a narrow "bottleneck" corresponding to the optic nerve, the layers before the bottleneck develop center-surround receptive fields, while without a bottleneck they develop oriented ones. This suggests that the retina's center-surround design may be a consequence of the optic nerve's limited capacity, as efficient coding theory predicts.

Event cameras. Engineers have built "neuromorphic" or "event-based" cameras, such as the dynamic vision sensor developed at the Institute of Neuroinformatics in Zurich (with work by Tobi Delbruck and colleagues), whose pixels, like retinal ON and OFF cells, report only changes in brightness, as asynchronous events, rather than full frames at a fixed rate. These sensors have very high temporal resolution and dynamic range and low power consumption, and they are used in robotics and high-speed vision. They are a direct engineering translation of retinal principles.

Normalization and gain control. The retina's adaptation to light level and contrast resembles normalization operations in neural networks and automatic exposure control in cameras. Divisive normalization, mentioned in section 2.3, was first proposed as a model of contrast gain control in the visual system, by David Heeger in the early 1990s, and the retina implements related forms of gain control.

Summary

- The retina is part of the brain and compresses information from about 100 million photoreceptors into about 1 million optic nerve fibers per eye.
- Photoreceptors hyperpolarize in response to light through an amplifying G-protein cascade; rods can detect single photons.
- ON and OFF bipolar pathways split signals into rectified increment and decrement channels.
- Hartline discovered lateral inhibition in Limulus; Kuffler (1953) described center-surround receptive fields in cat ganglion cells, modeled by a difference of Gaussians.
- Efficient coding theory explains center-surround filtering as redundancy reduction adapted to natural image statistics.
- The retina sends many parallel channels to the brain via the LGN to V1.
- Convolution, learned filters, event cameras, and normalization connect retinal processing to AI and engineering.
